cases.name: expert-summit-spending-disagreement
cases.description: Three recorded summit pages that disagree; the answer must give the 5% target and its split, and name who objected.

input.query: What did Northern Alliance leaders agree on defence spending, and who objected?

sources.title: Northern Alliance leaders adopt 5% spending goal
sources.text: Leaders of the Northern Alliance ended their two-day summit in Aldport with a joint defence pledge: every member will aim to spend 5 percent of national output on defence and defence-related activity by 2035. The communiqué splits the figure into two parts, 3.5 percent for core defence such as land, air, and naval forces, and 1.5 percent for related spending that includes resilience, cyber defence, and munitions production. Members committed to publish annual national plans from next year so that progress can be checked at every future summit, and the secretariat will compile a public scoreboard against the 2035 target. Delegations described the compromise as the price of keeping all twenty members inside one text rather than negotiating separate coalitions of the willing. Officials conceded that the goal is a political target with no enforcement mechanism; a member that falls short will face a review of its national plan but no sanction. The final communiqué notes that burden-sharing will be reviewed annually and that the related-spending definition may be tightened after the first round of national plans is submitted. Two leaders left the closing session early, and one skipped the group photograph, a sign of the arguments still to come over who counts what.

sources.title: Norland says 5% target is unrealistic
sources.text: Norland's prime minister told reporters after the Aldport summit that her country would not treat the 5 percent pledge as a binding timeline, calling it unrealistic for an economy already running a thin surplus. She cited Norland's current 2.1 percent as a sufficient level for its geography and alliance role, and argued that chasing the 2035 number would force cuts to pensions rather than produce tanks. According to her account, negotiators privately agreed that a member facing budget constraints could apply for a phased schedule, and she claimed that such an exemption was agreed in the final hours of the summit even though it does not appear in the published communiqué. Norland will still publish the required annual national plan, she said, but its first plan will project a flat budget with no date for reaching the core 3.5 percent. Her office released a one-line statement: targets without timelines are ambitions, and Norland reports to its own parliament first. Alliance officials in Aldport declined to confirm that any exemption exists, and the summit's joint press conference ended without the usual unanimous hand-raising photograph.

sources.title: Vestria backs target, asks for flexibility
sources.text: Vestria's delegation left the Aldport summit as one of the 5 percent target's loudest supporters, but its defence minister attached two caveats in a briefing aboard the flight home. First, Vestria disputes Norland's claim that any exemption was agreed: in his words, the communiqué is the whole agreement, and the communiqué has no opt-out clause, only a review process. Second, Vestria wants related spending defined broadly so that infrastructure counted toward defence readiness, including ports, bridges, and dual-use rail, can be included in the 1.5 percent tranche. The minister said Vestria's own national plan will reach the core 3.5 percent by 2032, three years ahead of the deadline, and that the remaining gap will be met by counting construction that is certified for military use. He warned against letting any member quietly reinterpret the deal, saying a target that bends for one country stops being a target for all twenty. Asked about the scoreboard idea, he welcomed it and proposed that the secretariat publish the figures every spring rather than only at summits.

expected.answer:
Northern Alliance leaders agreed to a joint defence spending goal of 5 percent of national output by 2035, which is divided into 3.5 percent for core defence and 1.5 percent for related spending such as resilience and cyber defence [Northern Alliance leaders adopt 5% spending goal](https://news.example/2026/06/alliance-summit-spending-target). However, Norland's prime minister objected to this target, calling it unrealistic for her country's economy and stating that it would lead to cuts in pensions rather than military spending. She mentioned that Norland's current spending level of 2.1 percent is sufficient and claimed that an exemption for members facing budget constraints was informally agreed upon, although this was not reflected in the official communiqué [Norland says 5% target is unrealistic](https://news.example/2026/06/norland-rejects-spending-target).

In contrast, Vestria supported the 5 percent target but disputed Norland's claim of an exemption, emphasizing that the communiqué is the complete agreement without any opt-out clause. Vestria's delegation also sought a broader definition of related spending to include infrastructure that supports defence readiness [Vestria backs target, asks for flexibility](https://news.example/2026/06/vestria-backs-target-with-caveats).
